note: Sanitized register for a PUBLIC repository. No exploit payloads, credentials, customer data or production topology. Each finding points at its remediation and its retest evidence; `evidenceHash` is the SHA-256 of the LF-normalized retest file and is re-verified by `npm run eval:phase99:readiness`.
externalFindingsChannel: Findings from an external review are NOT recorded here. See docs/security/phase99-finding-handling.md — they are handled in a private GitHub security advisory, and only counts plus hashes ever reach this repository.

findings.title: Unauthenticated endpoint wrote the authentication session cookie from the request body (session fixation)
findings.description: The cookie-consent endpoint keyed consent on `hermes_session`, which is SESSION_COOKIE — the signed authentication session that getCurrentUser() treats as the sole auth gate on most of the API — and set that cookie to a value taken from the request body. The endpoint requires no authentication, applies no origin check and had no rate limit, so an unauthenticated caller could plant a session of their choosing in another browser for one year on path=/.
findings.impact: Session fixation leading to account and tenant confusion: a victim operating under a planted session writes their work into the attacker's account and organization.
findings.remediationSummary: Consent now uses a dedicated, server-minted, opaque identifier cookie (hermes_consent_id) with a strict shape check. The authentication cookie is never read or written by this route, and a client-supplied sessionId is ignored outright.

findings.title: Live session tokens persisted and logged as consent keys, with an unauthenticated read of consent evidence
findings.description: Consent rows stored the caller's raw signed session token next to their user id, IP address and user agent, and both database helpers logged that token on failure. The read side looked a row up by an arbitrary caller-supplied cookie value and returned the whole row, so the endpoint answered as a lookup oracle for consent evidence; the anonymous fallback identifier was a millisecond timestamp and therefore enumerable.
findings.impact: Working session credentials at rest and in logs, plus anonymous disclosure of user id, IP address and user agent.
findings.remediationSummary: The stored key is now an opaque consent identifier that carries no authority. Responses project consent preferences only. Both log statements dropped the identifier. The recorded IP comes from resolveClientIp (X-Real-IP) instead of the client-controlled X-Forwarded-For.

findings.title: Mass assignment on the candidate self-service profile update
findings.description: The request body was cast with a TypeScript `as Partial<...>` assertion, which filters nothing at runtime, and forwarded whole into a Prisma update. AtsCandidate carries unique `email` and `userId` columns and an `applications` relation.
findings.impact: A self-registered candidate could claim another person's email to capture future applications, re-link identity via userId, or connect another candidate's application to themselves and then read its contents.
findings.remediationSummary: Explicit field allow-list copied key by key, matching the pattern already used by PATCH /api/academy/courses/[id]. Fields the client did not send are not invented.

findings.title: Public careers detail endpoint returned unpublished and cross-tenant job records
findings.description: The public detail route used the generic getJobById lookup, which filters only deletedAt, while the sibling list endpoint pinned status OPEN and isPublic true. Newly created postings default to DRAFT.
findings.impact: An anonymous caller holding a job id received the full record of a draft, closed or internal posting, including organizationId, internal requirements and salary bands.
findings.remediationSummary: The public route now enforces status OPEN and isPublic true and answers 404 otherwise, so it is not an existence oracle. The shared helper is unchanged for authenticated callers.

findings.title: Academy course detail endpoint had no authentication, tenant predicate or published check
findings.description: The detail endpoint looked a course up by primary key and returned it, while the sibling list endpoint required authentication, resolved the caller's active organization and served published courses only. The PATCH handler in the same file was correctly gated.
findings.impact: An anonymous caller holding a course id received another tenant's draft course, including organizationId, createdById, passingScore and enrollmentType.
findings.remediationSummary: The scope resolution was extracted into a shared module and the detail endpoint now applies the same three predicates as the list endpoint, answering 404 for a foreign or unpublished course.

findings.title: Academy assessment content readable anonymously across tenants
findings.description: Neither the quiz lookup nor the question lookup checked publication state or organization. Correct answers were already stripped, which is necessary but not sufficient.
findings.impact: An anonymous caller holding a quiz id received another tenant's unpublished exam: the full question set, passing score, attempt limit and time limit. Exam integrity as well as tenant isolation.
findings.remediationSummary: The quiz now inherits its visibility from its course: authentication is required, and the course's tenant and published predicates are applied before any question is returned.

findings.title: Raw SQL identifier interpolation guarded only by a comment
findings.description: Metadata filter keys were interpolated directly into a single-quoted JSON path inside a $queryRawUnsafe statement. Values were bound as parameters, but the key was not and could not be. The only control was a source comment asserting that callers pass developer-controlled keys.
findings.impact: Not reachable at the time of review — the sole production caller (/api/brain) passes no filters — but the invariant was unenforced, so any future caller forwarding a request-supplied filter object would have created a real injection.
findings.remediationSummary: Keys must now match a strict SQL-identifier pattern; a non-conforming key fails the search closed rather than being dropped, since silently ignoring a filter would widen the result set.

findings.title: Rate limit keyed on a client-controlled forwarding header
findings.description: The limiter hashed the left-most X-Forwarded-For entry. nginx appends to that header, so its left-most entry is whatever the client sent. This is the same bypass class Phase 93 fixed on the authentication routes.
findings.impact: Rotating the header per request gave every request its own bucket, defeating the cap entirely and allowing unbounded anonymous inserts.
findings.remediationSummary: Keying moved to resolveClientIp, which trusts only X-Real-IP — the header the reverse proxy overwrites with the real peer.

findings.title: Anonymous vendor onboarding had no abuse controls and stored a session credential
findings.description: The endpoint had no rate limit, no media-type check and no bounded body while accepting two 3000-character description fields per anonymous insert, unlike its direct analogue POST /api/careers/apply. It also read the raw authentication cookie and persisted it on the onboarding row.
findings.impact: Unbounded anonymous writes, and a live session credential at rest next to applicant contact details.
findings.remediationSummary: Added the vendor-apply rate-limit bucket, a JSON media-type check and a bounded body read, mirroring the careers application. The session token is no longer read or stored.

findings.title: Unbounded client-controlled page size on a public listing endpoint
findings.description: The limit and page query parameters were passed straight through to Prisma take and skip with a three-level include, with no ceiling and no rejection of non-numeric input. Sibling public endpoints already clamp.
findings.impact: An anonymous caller could request an arbitrarily large page and run an unbounded join.
findings.remediationSummary: Page size clamped to 100 and page number to 1000; non-integer or negative input falls back to the default instead of reaching the query as NaN.

findings.title: Unbounded cross-tenant table scan reachable from anonymous derived-graph endpoints
findings.affectedSurface: src/lib/storage/knowledge-repository.ts, reachable via GET /api/eng-graph/* and GET /api/operations/*
findings.description: The knowledge repository lists rows with no where clause and no take, then filters to published records in JavaScript. The engineering-graph builder is not memoized and its nine consumers are force-dynamic with no rate limit, so each anonymous request drives one full-table read plus a bounded case read.
findings.impact: Availability and cost, not disclosure: unpublished rows are filtered out before the response, but every anonymous request loads all tenants' rows into memory. No cross-tenant data is returned.
findings.remediationSummary: NOT REMEDIATED IN PHASE 99. Adding pagination or a published-only predicate to a shared repository changes what the derived graph contains, which is a product-behaviour decision rather than a contained security fix. Recorded for owner decision with two candidate remediations: push the published predicate and a bounded take into the query, or memoize the builder behind a short TTL and rate-limit the nine anonymous consumers.

findings.title: Anonymous analysis endpoint parsed an unbounded body with no rate limit
findings.description: Field-level bounds were applied by Zod only after the whole body had been parsed, and there was no rate limit or media-type check, unlike the sibling public analysis endpoint.
findings.impact: Resource exhaustion on an anonymous endpoint. The analysis itself reaches no database, provider or model, so no data or paid inference was exposed.
findings.remediationSummary: Added a rate-limit bucket, a JSON media-type check and a bounded body read, matching POST /api/copilot/demo.

findings.title: Certificate verification reported expired certificates as valid
findings.description: The verification endpoint returned valid true unconditionally. The expiry date was echoed in the response but never compared against the current time.
findings.impact: A certificate whose expiry had passed still verified as valid, with the holder's real name attached.
findings.remediationSummary: Validity is now derived from the expiry date; a null expiry means the certificate does not expire and stays valid.

findings.title: Site allow-list bypassed by an explicit siteId on the asset listing
findings.description: The Phase 43 site allow-list was applied only when no siteId was supplied. A supplied siteId therefore REPLACED the allow-list instead of narrowing it, so a member holding a UserSite grant for one site could read another site’s assets in the same organization by naming that site in the query string. The item route (assets/[id]) enforced the boundary correctly, so the control was defeated purely by choosing a different URL.
findings.impact: Same-organization, cross-SITE read of the full asset inventory by any member with the view_industrial permission and at least one site grant.
findings.remediationSummary: The allow-list is now always applied when present; a requested site must be a member of it or the query returns nothing and is never issued.

findings.title: Site allow-list bypassed by an explicit siteId on the gateway listing
findings.description: Same if/else shape as the asset listing: an explicit siteId replaced the allow-list rather than narrowing it.
findings.impact: Same-organization, cross-SITE read of gateway inventory including apiKeyId and metadata.
findings.remediationSummary: The allow-list is now always applied when present; a site outside it returns nothing.

findings.title: Site allow-list bypassed by a gatewayId filter on the connector listing
findings.description: The site allow-list was skipped whenever a gatewayId was supplied, so naming a gateway belonging to another site returned that site’s connector rows.
findings.impact: Same-organization, cross-SITE disclosure of connector configuration, which carries OPC UA and MQTT endpoint and connection material.
findings.remediationSummary: The gateway filter and the site allow-list are now independent predicates and both are applied.

findings.title: Asset analytics applied no site allow-list, and its score queries were invalid
findings.description: The only route under /api/industrial that never resolved the caller’s permitted sites, so its aggregate crossed the site boundary its siblings enforce. Separately, the same where clause (containing siteId) was reused for assetRiskScore and assetHealthHistory, neither of which has a siteId column, so any request with ?siteId= raised a Prisma validation error and answered an unhandled 500.
findings.impact: Cross-site aggregate disclosure (asset counts, status distribution, average risk score) and a guaranteed 500 on any site-filtered request.
findings.remediationSummary: The route now resolves getAllowedSiteIds like its siblings; the aggregate intersects org-scoped score rows with the visible asset set, and the score models are queried by organization only.

findings.title: Create handlers wrote a client-supplied siteId with no site-level authorization
findings.description: The three create handlers took siteId from the body and wrote it with no requireSiteActor or requireSitePermission, while the corresponding PATCH handlers enforced both. Cross-organization writes were already prevented because the row is stamped with the caller’s organizationId.
findings.impact: A member holding a grant for one site could create assets, gateways and connectors on another site in the same organization, and would then be unable to edit them.
findings.remediationSummary: The create handlers now authorise the target site with the same requireSiteActor and requireSitePermission predicates the update handlers use.

findings.title: Anonymous write endpoints parsed unbounded request bodies
findings.description: Six unauthenticated endpoints (four credential flows, the public lead form and cookie consent) called req.json() with no byte ceiling. A rate limit bounds how many requests are accepted, not how large each one may be.
findings.impact: Resource exhaustion on anonymous endpoints. No data exposure.
findings.remediationReference: src/lib/security/request-guards.ts; the six affected route files
findings.remediationSummary: Added readBoundedJson with a shared SMALL_JSON_BODY_BYTES ceiling and applied it to every anonymous JSON write; cookie consent also gained a rate-limit bucket.
